title: CCPA Fines ExportersIndia Rs 10 Lakh Over Unverified Listings of Explosive Picric Acid
meta_description: The Central Consumer Protection Authority penalises Weblink, which runs ExportersIndia.com, for facilitating unchecked online listings of picric acid.
bench: Central Consumer Protection Authority, New Delhi
citation: Case No. CCPA-2/54/2026-CCPA, order dated 10 September 2026
body: Picric acid is not a chemical any marketplace should let a stranger buy with a few clicks. It is a notified explosive under the Explosives Act, 1884, specifically under Notification No. GSR 625(E) dated 7 August 1983, and its sale is meant to be tightly controlled through licensing under the Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organisation, commonly known as PESO. Weblink Private Limited, which runs the B2B marketplace ExportersIndia.com, let sellers list it anyway, and the Central Consumer Protection Authority has fined the company Rs 10 lakh for allowing that to happen.

The CCPA's order, dated 10 September 2026, found that listings for picric acid on the platform lacked the basic safeguards that ought to accompany the sale of a notified explosive. There was no adequate disclosure that the seller held a valid PESO licence, no verification of whether the prospective buyer was authorised to purchase the substance at all, and no warning language of the kind one would expect for a chemical that can detonate under the wrong conditions. The authority treated these gaps as more than a labelling slip. They went to whether the platform was facilitating transactions in a controlled, dangerous substance without any of the checks that controlled status is supposed to require.

Weblink's defence leaned on the nature of its platform rather than on the listings themselves. The company argued that ExportersIndia.com operates as a non-transactional business-to-business information and directory service, and that actual transactions take place independently between buyers and sellers once they connect through the site. On that reading, the company's role stops at introducing parties to each other, and any failure of verification belongs to the seller and buyer, not to the platform that merely hosted their listing.

The CCPA was not persuaded, and the Rs 10 lakh penalty reflects that. A platform that hosts and indexes product listings for a notified explosive, searchable by any visitor, cannot treat itself as a bystander to what happens once a buyer finds the listing. If the platform's business model depends on connecting buyers to sellers of hazardous and controlled goods, the authority's position is that some responsibility for screening those listings travels with the business, whatever the platform calls itself in its terms of service.

This order did not arise in isolation. It traces back to a wider CCPA crackdown that began in May 2026, when the authority opened cases against several major platforms, including IndiaMART, Justdial, Sigma-Aldrich India, Dial4Trade and ExportersIndia itself, over the online sale of hazardous chemicals and explosives. Eight notices went out across these platforms as part of that sweep, of which the Weblink order is one outcome. Other platforms named in the same investigation have faced their own separate proceedings and, in at least one other instance, their own penalty for similar conduct involving listings of hazardous substances.

For e-commerce marketplaces operating in India, particularly B2B directory and listing platforms that have historically treated themselves as mere intermediaries under the old safe-harbour logic of the Information Technology Act, this order is a signal that the Consumer Protection Act and its e-commerce rules are being read more strictly where the goods involved carry genuine public safety risk. A platform cannot rely on a disclaimer describing itself as non-transactional once a regulator decides that the real-world consequence of its listings is unverified access to an explosive. Chemical, pharmaceutical and industrial-goods marketplaces operating India-facing listings would do well to audit their categories against India's notified hazardous and controlled substances list now, rather than waiting for their own show-cause notice to arrive.

The pattern across the wider May 2026 sweep is also worth watching closely, since this is unlikely to be the last order to come out of it. Where the CCPA has already proceeded against one platform in a group of similarly placed marketplaces, the remaining platforms named in the same set of notices should expect their own orders to follow a broadly similar template, with the same emphasis on seller licensing disclosure, buyer eligibility checks and adequate hazard warnings. Waiting to see how another platform's proceeding concludes before fixing one's own listing practices is a slow way of discovering what the regulator already expects.

A ten lakh rupee penalty is not, on its own, a figure large enough to force a change in business practice for most established marketplaces, and in-house counsel at these platforms should read the order for that reason rather than for the fine itself. The reputational and regulatory signal matters more than the quantum here. Once a regulator has drawn a line around what counts as adequate verification for hazardous-goods listings, repeat violations after this order, or similar violations by a platform that watched this proceeding play out and did nothing, invite a different and considerably less forgiving response the next time around.
why_it_matters: B2B and classifieds-style marketplaces have long argued that listing a product is different from selling it, and that verification obligations fall on the transacting parties rather than the platform. This order signals that the CCPA will not accept that distinction where the listed goods are notified explosives or other controlled hazardous substances, and will impose penalties directly on the platform for inadequate seller and buyer verification. Any India-facing marketplace carrying industrial chemical or explosive-adjacent product categories should treat this as a trigger to review listing controls before the next enforcement sweep reaches them.
card_summary: CCPA fines ExportersIndia Rs 10 lakh for hosting unverified picric acid listings, rejecting the platform's defence that it is merely a non-transactional directory service.
card_tip: A 'non-transactional directory' defence will not shield a marketplace from CCPA penalties if it lists notified explosives or hazardous chemicals without seller licence and buyer verification checks.
verification_notes: The order date, case number, penalty amount, the picric acid notification reference, and Weblink's non-transactional-platform defence are confirmed by TaxGuru's report; the broader May 2026 CCPA crackdown covering IndiaMART, Justdial, Sigma-Aldrich India, Dial4Trade and ExportersIndia, and the eight notices issued, are independently corroborated by Daily Pioneer and Latestly. No source gave the specific number of picric acid listings found on the platform or the identity of the seller accounts involved, so neither detail is stated. The precise statutory provision of the Consumer Protection Act and e-commerce rules relied on for the penalty was not specified in any source and is therefore not asserted here beyond the general reference to the Act and its e-commerce rules.
